title: Economics
description: Free Economics study guide: 8 units, 320+ practice questions, 80 flashcards, quick reference, memory tricks, and a full practice exam. Completely free.

units.name: Scarcity & Opportunity Cost

concepts.intro: Unlimited wants meet limited resources — the core problem economics solves.
b: Scarcity forces choice; every choice has a cost even when 'free'
Factors: land (natural resources), labor (human work), capital (tools/machines), entrepreneurship (organizing risk)
Goods vs services; tangible vs intangible outputs
Shortage = temporary; scarcity = permanent condition

concepts.intro: The real cost of anything is what you gave up to get it.
b: Opportunity cost = value of the NEXT-BEST alternative forgone
Trade-off = giving up one thing for another (broader term)
Money cost vs time cost vs foregone experience all count
'There's no such thing as a free lunch' (TINSTAAFL)

concepts.intro: A curve showing maximum output combos of two goods with fixed resources.
b: Points ON the curve = efficient; INSIDE = underutilization; OUTSIDE = unattainable now
Straight-line PPF = constant opportunity costs; bowed-out = increasing costs (law of increasing opportunity cost)
Growth shifts the whole curve outward (more resources/technology)
Moving along the curve shows trade-offs: more guns, fewer butter

concepts.intro: Every economy must answer: what, how, and for whom to produce.
b: Traditional economy: custom answers (subsistence, stable, stagnant)
Command economy: government decides (Cuba, North Korea)
Market economy: buyers/sellers decide via prices (US is mixed, market-leaning)
Mixed economies blend; most real nations live on the spectrum

keyFacts: Opportunity cost = NEXT-BEST alternative given up
PPF inside = inefficient, on = efficient, outside = impossible (today)
Increasing opportunity cost bows the PPF outward
traps: Opportunity cost isn't ALL alternatives — only the next-best single one
A free concert still costs your time (scarcity never sleeps)
Growth moves the PPF outward; moving ALONG the curve is not growth

units.name: Supply & Demand

concepts.intro: Price up, quantity demanded down — the demand curve slopes downward.
b: Law of demand: inverse price-quantity relationship
Movement ALONG the curve = price change; SHIFT of the curve = determinants changed
Demand shifters: income (normal vs inferior goods), tastes, related goods' prices (substitutes/complements), expectations, number of buyers
Substitutes rise together (Coke↔Pepsi); complements move opposite (gas↔SUVs)

concepts.intro: Producers offer more at higher prices — upward-sloping supply.
b: Law of supply: direct relationship between price and quantity supplied
Supply shifters: input costs, technology, taxes/subsidies, expectations, number of sellers
Technology lowers costs → supply shifts RIGHT
Weather/catastrophe can shift agricultural supply left instantly

concepts.intro: Where curves cross, markets clear — no shortage, no surplus.
b: Equilibrium price = quantity demanded exactly equals quantity supplied
Price ABOVE equilibrium → surplus → downward pressure
Price BELOW equilibrium → shortage → upward pressure
Markets self-correct toward equilibrium unless price-controlled

concepts.intro: Government interference creates persistent gaps.
b: Price ceiling below equilibrium (rent control) → chronic shortage
Price floor above equilibrium (minimum wage debate) → potential surplus (unemployment)
Binding controls require being on the 'wrong side' of equilibrium
Black markets often emerge under binding ceilings

keyFacts: Price change = movement ALONG a curve; other factors SHIFT the curve
Surplus above equilibrium, shortage below
Ceiling (max price) below EQ → shortage; floor (min price) above EQ → surplus
traps: Change in QUANTITY demanded (movement) ≠ change in DEMAND (shift)
Demand curve slopes DOWN; supply UP — flipping them is the classic error
Minimum wage is a FLOOR not a ceiling — rent control is the ceiling example

units.name: Market Structures

concepts.intro: Many tiny sellers, identical products, zero barriers — pure price takers.
b: Characteristics: many buyers/sellers, homogeneous product, free entry/exit, perfect information
Firms are PRICE TAKERS — no market power at all
Examples: agricultural commodities approximating it (wheat, corn)
Long-run economic profit trends to zero via entry

concepts.intro: One seller controls the market behind high barriers.
b: Barriers: legal (patents), natural (utilities' infrastructure), resource control
Monopolists are PRICE MAKERS (within demand limits)
Can charge higher prices, produce less than socially optimal
Natural monopoly = cheapest with ONE provider due to huge fixed costs

concepts.intro: The middle grounds where most real businesses live.
b: Oligopoly: few big firms, interdependent pricing (airlines, telecoms); collusion/kinked-demand risks
Monopolistic competition: MANY sellers, DIFFERENTIATED products, easy entry (restaurants, clothing brands)
Product differentiation gives slight pricing power via branding
Non-price competition (ads, features) dominates monopolistic competition

concepts.intro: Markets sometimes misallocate on their own.
b: Externalities: spillover costs (pollution) or benefits (education/vaccines)
Public goods: non-excludable + non-rival (national defense) — markets undersupply them
Information asymmetry: used-car problem (adverse selection)
Government responds with taxes, subsidies, regulation

keyFacts: Perfect competition = price TAKER; monopoly = price MAKER
Monopolistic competition = many firms + differentiated products
Public goods (defense) get undersupplied by free markets
traps: Oligopoly needs FEW firms — three coffee shops on a block isn't one by headcount alone
Differentiation (not product identity) defines monopolistic competition
Externalities are THIRD-PARTY effects, not buyer/seller harms

units.name: Business Organizations & Labor

concepts.intro: Simple ownership structures trade liability for ease.
b: Sole prop: one owner, full control, unlimited personal liability, easy taxes (pass-through)
General partnership: shared ownership/management/debt — partners jointly liable
Limited partnership: silent limited partners cap risk
Biggest weakness of both: personal assets exposed to business debts

concepts.intro: Incorporation creates a legal person that shields owners.
b: Corporation: shareholders own, board governs, officers run — LIMITED liability
Stocks = ownership shares; dividends = profit distributions; double taxation drawback
S-corp/LLC hybrids blend pass-through taxes with liability protection
Franchise: license a proven brand/model (McDonald's) — fees + standards

concepts.intro: Wages emerge from supply and demand for skills.
b: Demand for labor = derived demand (from demand for the product)
Skilled labor commands premiums: education/training as investment in human capital
Unions negotiate collectively: wages, benefits, conditions; strikes = ultimate leverage
Minimum wage debates center on floors in this market

concepts.intro: Economies breathe in expansions and contractions.
b: Cycle phases: expansion → peak → contraction (recession) → trough → recovery
Recession rule-of-thumb: two consecutive quarters of falling GDP
Leading indicators predict (stock market, building permits); lagging confirm (unemployment duration)
GDP = total value of final goods/services produced domestically in a period

keyFacts: Corporation's superpower = LIMITED liability for owners
Labor demand is DERIVED from product demand
Recession ≈ two consecutive negative GDP quarters
traps: LLCs protect personal assets; sole props don't — mixing them up is costly advice
GDP counts FINAL goods only — intermediate sales would double-count
Unemployment rate ≠ percentage of population without jobs — it's of the LABOR FORCE

units.name: Money, Banking & the Fed

concepts.intro: Money is whatever does money's three jobs well.
b: Functions: medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value
Commodity money (gold) vs fiat money (US dollar — valuable by government decree/trust)
Characteristics: durable, portable, divisible, uniform, limited supply, acceptable
Hyperinflation destroys store-of-value function (Weimar Germany, Zimbabwe)

concepts.intro: Banks create money by lending most of what you deposit.
b: Fractional reserve system: banks keep a fraction, lend the rest
Money multiplier ≈ 1/reserve ratio (10% reserve → up to 10x expansion)
Deposit insurance (FDIC) prevents bank runs from rumor
Interest: banks pay you less than they charge borrowers — the spread is their profit

concepts.intro: The US central bank: independent, dual-mandated, decentralized.
b: Dual mandate: price stability + maximum employment
Board of Governors (7, presidential appointments) + 12 regional banks
FOMC conducts open-market operations — the main policy lever
Fed is NOT part of the executive branch — independence insulates politics

concepts.intro: The Fed moves the economy with three levers.
b: Open market operations: buy bonds → inject money (expansionary); sell → drain (contractionary)
Reserve requirement changes (rarely used — too blunt)
Discount rate: rate Fed charges banks to borrow — signals stance
Expansionary tools fight recessions; contractionary fights inflation

keyFacts: Three functions of money: exchange medium, unit of account, store of value
Fed buys bonds → money supply expands; sells → contracts
Fiat money's value rests on trust + government decree
traps: The Fed is NOT a government agency under the President — quasi-independent matters
Printing more money doesn't create wealth — it can dilute it (inflation)
Reserve requirements change rarely; OMOs are the daily driver

units.name: Personal Finance

concepts.intro: Income minus expenses minus savings should equal zero — on purpose.
b: Pay-yourself-first: treat savings as a fixed expense (aim 10–20%)
Fixed vs variable expenses; emergency fund = 3–6 months of costs first
Needs vs wants triage keeps variable spending honest
Zero-based budget assigns every dollar a job before the month starts

concepts.intro: Borrowed money amplifies outcomes both ways.
b: Credit score drivers: payment history (biggest), amounts owed/utilization, length, new credit, mix
Utilization under ~30% protects your score
APR compounds against you: minimum-payment traps stretch debt for decades
Good debt buys appreciating/earning assets (education, mortgage); bad debt funds consumption

concepts.intro: Compounding is the engine — direction just depends on which side you're on.
b: Simple interest = principal × rate × time
Compound interest earns interest ON interest: A=P(1+r/n)^(nt)
Rule of 72: years to double ≈ 72 ÷ interest rate
Start-early advantage: $1,000 at 8% from age 18 beats $3,000 at 28 by retirement

concepts.intro: Risk and return are conjoined twins; diversification tames them.
b: Stocks = ownership (volatile, higher expected return); bonds = loans (steadier, lower return)
Diversification spreads risk — index funds automate it cheaply
Risk tolerance + time horizon determine allocation
Time IN the market beats timing the market for most investors

keyFacts: Rule of 72: doubling time ≈ 72 ÷ annual % return
Payment history dominates credit scores
Compound interest rewards starters over savers-later
traps: Minimum credit-card payments mostly service interest — principal barely moves
A 'free' trial that needs a card isn't free — it's auto-renewal bait
High return ALWAYS pairs with high risk; guaranteed high returns are scams

units.name: Government & the Economy

concepts.intro: Governments fund themselves through structures with different fairness logics.
b: Progressive tax: rate rises with income (federal income tax brackets)
Regressive tax: takes a LARGER share from lower incomes (sales taxes)
Proportional/flat tax: same percentage for everyone
Principles: benefit received vs ability to pay; equity vs efficiency tension

concepts.intro: Congress + President steer spending and taxes.
b: Expansionary fiscal (recession): raise spending, cut taxes → deficit-financed stimulus
Contractionary fiscal (inflation): cut spending, raise taxes → cool demand
Multiplier effect: initial spending ripples through the economy
Deficits = yearly gap; debt = accumulated total — national debt is the sum of deficits

concepts.intro: The Fed's levers (Unit 5) aim at the same targets from the money side.
b: Easy money (expansionary): buy bonds, cut rates → borrowing rises
Tight money (contractionary): sell bonds, raise rates → inflation cools
Lags: monetary policy acts faster to implement but works through slower channels
Policy mix matters: conflicting fiscal+monetary steps can cancel

concepts.intro: When prices lie about true costs, government corrects.
b: Negative externality (pollution) → per-unit taxes/regulation internalize costs
Positive externality (vaccination) → subsidies encourage output
Direct regulation vs market-based instruments (cap-and-trade)
Public goods require taxation because free-riders dodge payment

keyFacts: Sales taxes are regressive; federal income tax progressive
Expansionary fiscal = spend more + tax less (deficits grow)
Pollution = negative externality → tax or regulate it
traps: Debt ≠ deficit — deficit is annual flow; debt is the accumulated stock
Contractionary policy fights INFLATION, not recession — mixing these flips answers
A flat tax is proportional, not regressive — percentage constant even if burden feels heavier low-income

units.name: International Trade & Globalization

concepts.intro: Trade happens because of RELATIVE efficiency, not absolute skill.
b: Absolute advantage: can produce more total output with same resources
Comparative advantage: LOWER opportunity cost producer should specialize
Both sides gain when each specializes in their comparative advantage and trades
Even the country worse at EVERYTHING still has a comparative advantage in something

concepts.intro: Protectionism taxes or caps trade — consumers pay.
b: Tariff = tax on imports → raises domestic price, protects local producers, hurts consumers
Quota = quantity limit on imports — similar consumer cost via scarcity
Deadweight loss: gains that vanish under trade barriers
Retaliation risks trade wars shrinking everyone's pie

concepts.intro: Currency prices steer trade flows automatically.
b: Appreciating dollar: imports cheaper for Americans, exports pricier abroad → trade deficit widens
Depreciating dollar reverses both effects
Trade deficit = imports > exports (not inherently 'losing') — offset by capital flows
Purchasing power parity: identical baskets should cost the same across currencies long-run

concepts.intro: Integration delivers growth AND dislocation simultaneously.
b: Gains: cheaper goods, bigger markets, technology diffusion, specialization gains
Costs: manufacturing job shifts, wage pressure on unskilled labor, cultural homogenization anxiety
Development spectrum: developing nations gain factory jobs → climb value chain (Korea, Taiwan models)
Institutions grease trade: WTO rules, regional blocs (USMCA, EU)

keyFacts: Comparative advantage = lowest OPPORTUNITY COST, wins trade logic
Tariff raises import prices; consumers bear most of it
Strong dollar helps buyers of imports, hurts exporters
traps: Absolute advantage doesn't determine trade patterns — comparative advantage does
A trade deficit isn't a scoreboard loss — it reflects investment flows too
Tariffs help protected producers but cost consumers MORE than producers gain (deadweight loss)

PART_B2.e: Ceilings create shortages — surpluses come from floors.

PART_B2.e: Few rivals matching moves signals interdependent oligopoly behavior.

o: False — Congress funds via taxes/borrowing; the Fed conducts monetary policy independently
PART_B2.e: Fiscal = Congress; monetary = Fed. Independence separates them.

PART_B2.e: Principal-focused extra payments cut compounding interest — fastest debt decay.

PART_B2.q: Why might economists OPPOSE a new tariff even when it 'saves' 500 steel jobs?
o: Consumer losses + deadweight loss typically exceed producer/job gains
PART_B2.e: Concentrated visible gains hide diffuse larger consumer costs.

PART_B2.e: X's truck costs 2 cars; Y's costs only 0.2 — Y's opportunity cost is lower.

PART_B2.e: Safety buffer precedes market exposure — shocks without debt.

PART_C.q: Synthesis: A senator proposes BOTH a national rent-control program AND expanded construction subsidies. Analyze the combined market outcome using supply/demand + price-control theory. Strongest analysis:
o: Short-run renters gain from capped rents, but unless subsidies shift LONG-RUN supply right substantially, ceilings create persistent shortages, queues, and quality decline — subsidy size/timing determines whether supply growth outruns distortion.
PART_C.e: Applies ceiling-shortage logic + supply-shift remedy; evaluates whether the shift outweighs the distortion — real synthesis.

PART_C.q: Essay prompt: 'Should the US adopt a significantly higher federal minimum wage?' Build the argument architecture citing elasticity reasoning. Strongest skeleton:
o: Thesis: moderate increase optimizes gains with minimal job loss WHERE labor demand is inelastic (monopsony markets); concede: in competitive low-margin sectors, elastic demand risks hours cuts; resolve: regional phase-ins + small-business credits address heterogeneity.
No because rich people say so.
PART_C.e: Uses elasticity as the decision hinge, concedes the strongest counter, and resolves with mechanism-aware policy design.
